name: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1804 (Treaty of Tellico)
nations: Cherokee (Tsalagi), today the Cherokee Nation, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and the United Keetoowah Band of Cherokee Indians
promises: The Cherokee ceded a strip four miles deep along the Georgia line that took in all the plantations of Wafford's Settlement (Article 1).
On signing, the United States would deliver $5,000 in useful goods or money, at the Cherokee's choice (Article 2).
The United States would also deliver $1,000 a year in goods or money, in addition to the annuity already promised (Article 2).
landTaken: Royce Area 52 in Georgia, the Wafford's Settlement tract described in Article 1.
compensation: The treaty consideration was $5,000 on signing and $1,000 a year (Article 2). Whether these were paid between 1804 and the 1824 proclamation was not traced.
today: The Statutes at Large print the treaty among the 1824 treaties with a proclamation date of May 17, 1824, twenty years after signing. No Indian Claims Commission or court ruling specific to this cession was found.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's history says successive treaties with the British Crown and then the United States cut down the Cherokee Nation's original territory, and that further cessions confirmed in an 1819 treaty left most of the remaining Cherokee land in Georgia.

sources.title: Treaty with the Cherokee, 1804 (Kappler, vol. 2, p. 73)
sources.publisher: Oklahoma State University Libraries, Tribal Treaties Database

sources.title: Articles of a Treaty between the United States of America and the Cherokee Indians, October 24, 1804 (7 Stat. 228)

openQuestions: The OSU Tribal Treaties Database page prints the citation as '7 Stat., 288'; the Statutes at Large scan shows the treaty at 7 Stat. 228, which is used here.

The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians settled Dockets 282-A to 282-L in 1972 for $1,855,254.50, a compromise covering its share of Cherokee cessions under treaties of 1785 to 1835 (28 Ind. Cl. Comm. 386). The docket-by-treaty list was not readable in the scanned 1959 severance order, so whether this treaty was among them is unconfirmed; even if so it would be a settlement, not a finding.
Why the treaty went unproclaimed for twenty years, and whether the goods and annuity were delivered in that time, was not researched.
No account of this treaty by a Cherokee nation was found in this pass.
